title: Stop Waiting for the Perfect App

slides.title: Title
slides.notes:
B00 · Title
[Start the show before people arrive. The title plays once, then runs straight into the holding loop by itself.]

B00 · Holding loop (loops while the room arrives)
As people come in:
Welcome, everyone. Grab a seat, open the laptop you brought, and check you can access at least one AI available in your region. We will explore Automate, WebApp and Agents together.

[When everyone's in, click to begin.]
▶ Click: the fern.

slides.title: Recursion
slides.notes:
B01 · Recursion
Nobody drew this fern.
A computer took four tiny rules and fed each answer back in as the next question, over and over, and the leaf appeared.
Zoom in and you find the whole fern again. And again.
That's recursion: the same rule, applied to its own output.

▶ Click: the rule comes out of the fern.

slides.title: Same rule
slides.notes:
B02a · Same rule (plays, then holds on the lungs)
Watch the rule underneath the fern.
[As it becomes rivers] The same rule makes a coastline: rivers splitting into smaller rivers, and every bay with smaller bays inside it.
[As it turns into lungs] Turn it over and it's inside you: a pair of lungs. One tube splitting in two, and again, and again.

▶ Click: a brain cell.

slides.title: Same rule
slides.notes:
B02b · A brain cell
And it's the cell you're thinking with right now. It branches the same way, gathers signals, and passes one on.
A second thought is that loop on purpose: your own thinking, fed back in.

▶ Click: Now, AI.

slides.title: Same rule
slides.notes:
B02c · Now, AI
Now, AI.
It's loosely modelled on those cells: layers of simple connections.
It makes a guess, checks how far off it was, adjusts its connections, and goes round again.
The same rule, applied to its own output.

▶ Click: the turn.

slides.title: The turn
slides.notes:
B03 · The turn
If the machine recurses on knowledge, the value isn't in knowing.
[Pause. Let it land. This slide is meant to be still.]
And it's not just me saying that.

▶ Click: Seymour Papert.

slides.title: Seymour
slides.notes:
B04a · Seymour Papert
This is Seymour Papert.
I learnt to code visually through Turtle Art. It allowed me to understand recursion in a way I couldn't through the mathematics alone.
[Let his portrait draw first. Follow its line into the recursive tree. Use the visual to tell your own learning story; save the Lineage introduction for the next scene.]

▶ Click: the Lineage card activity.

slides.title: Lineage
slides.notes:
B04b · Lineage · Card activity
[Let the portrait-and-tree line become the tangled pattern and resolve into a card back. Introduce Lineage after the card is recognisable, then explain the activity as the text arrives.]
In your groups, shuffle the cards and lay out ten cards face down.
Two of those ten cards are our jokers: Elon Musk and Rick Rubin.
Take turns turning over the cards.
[Let the sequential card flips demonstrate taking turns; the cards then return face down. Hold while the groups do the activity. Point to the highlighted word turns. The link to LLM turns is for your later explanation; do not introduce an extra scoring rule, stopping rule or reveal it automatically.]

▶ Click: MIT.

slides.title: Watershed
slides.notes:
B04 · Watershed
[Let the top-left Lineage card grow and flip into the MIT paper. Begin the next concept once the poster has opened and its quote arrives.]
In August, MIT's president, Sally Kornbluth, wrote to her whole community that AI in education is a watershed moment for MIT.
And she quoted her own AI committee: responding to it is not an optional exercise.
Their report points to three things: education that is AI-aware, people and community, and continuous reflection.

▶ Click: what MIT's students say.

slides.title: Three numbers
slides.notes:
B05a · Three numbers
Here's what MIT's own undergraduates said, in a survey by The Tech, their student paper, late last year.
46 per cent use an AI chatbot every day.
90 per cent worry they're becoming over-reliant on it.

▶ Click: the third number.

slides.title: Three numbers
slides.notes:
B05b · The third number
And only 25 per cent think MIT is preparing them to use AI.
[Pause.]
That's MIT. It's worth asking how our students would answer.

▶ Click: so what do we teach?

slides.title: So we teach
slides.notes:
B05Ta · So we teach
So what do we teach?
Thinking routines.
And creativity.
That's where the value is now.

▶ Click: why we start with reflection.

slides.title: So we teach
slides.notes:
B05Tb · Why we start with reflection
This is why we start with reflection: to find the problems worth solving, before anyone touches a tool.

▶ Click: the loop we'll run today.

slides.title: The loop, first
slides.notes:
B05L · The loop, first
Here's the loop we'll run today, twice.
Find a barrier. Sketch it. Write the prompt. Build it. Test it. Then go round again.
Hold on to this shape. You'll see it again at the end.

▶ Click: the question.

slides.title: The question
slides.notes:
B06 · The question
Homa Tavangar puts it this way: the question is no longer "What do you know?"
It's this.
What problems do you want to solve?
[Pause.]

▶ Click: two kinds of problem.

slides.title: Algorithmic vs heuristic
slides.notes:
B07-1 · Algorithmic vs heuristic
There are two kinds of problem.
Algorithmic problems have a known procedure. Follow the steps, get the answer.
Heuristic problems don't. There's no procedure, just rules of thumb, judgment and trial. You know you've arrived when you look at it.

▶ Click: which one AI has eaten.

slides.title: Algorithmic vs heuristic
slides.notes:
B07-2 · The payoff
AI has eaten the first kind.
And every hard problem in your classroom is on the right.
That's why nobody has built the tool you need, and why you're the only one who can.

▶ Click: Rick Rubin.

slides.title: Rick Rubin
slides.notes:
B07a · Rick Rubin
[Follow the heuristic line as it continues into Rick Rubin's portrait. Explain his relationship to vibe coding in your own words; then connect Automate, WebApp and Agents to the three workshop exercises.]
[Background source for preparation: Rick Rubin's The Way of Code, https://www.thewayofcode.com/ . The portrait and story reference are retained from the Lineage project.]

▶ Click: warm-up, Round 1 — through the existing ribbon transition.

slides.title: Round 1
slides.notes:
B08 · Round 1
Let's warm up. This comes from Creative Hustle, by Olatunde Sobomehin and Sam Seidel.
Write the most ridiculous word you can think of.
Now stand up and find someone you don't work with.
Pitch them a product with that name. You have three minutes.

▶ Click: start the three-minute Round 1 timer.

slides.title: Round 1 timer
slides.notes:
B08a · Round 1 timer
[The persistent step-three reminder reads: Pitch a product with that name.]
[The countdown runs from 03:00 to 00:00 over exactly 180 seconds. Give the room the full activity time. The completed picture and 00:00 hold until you advance.]
[The wordless line moves through the song’s imagery, then finishes on Jay-Z’s face from the supplied reference. Background music: the supplied 99 Problems instrumental, cropped to the first three minutes, with a two-second fade to silence at the end.]

▶ Click: Round 2.

slides.title: Round 2
slides.notes:
B09 · Round 2
Round 2. Now write your real classroom problem, in one sentence.
Find a new partner. Pitch each other a solution. You have four minutes.

▶ Click: start the four-minute Round 2 timer.

slides.title: Round 2 timer
slides.notes:
B09a · Round 2 timer
[The countdown runs from 04:00 to 00:00 over exactly 240 seconds. The third instruction remains visible: Pitch each other a solution. Give the room the full activity time, then bring everyone back to their seats.]
[The line moves through city and bridge imagery and resolves into the supplied Red Hot Chili Peppers illustration. The supplied Under the Bridge instrumental plays for four minutes, with a two-second closing fade.]

▶ Click: deficit.

slides.title: Deficit
slides.notes:
B10-1 · Deficit
Here's how most of us write a problem down:
They can't organise their writing.
That's a deficit. It lives in the student.

▶ Click: the same problem as a barrier.

slides.title: Barrier
slides.notes:
B10-2 · Barrier
Now the same thing as a barrier:
The organising has to happen in their head at the same time as the writing.
Same student. Different problem. Only one of them is yours to fix.
[Optional: it's the same move as our UDL work. The barrier is in the design, not the learner.]

▶ Click: introduce Apple Shortcuts.

slides.title: Apple Shortcuts
slides.notes:
B10a · Apple Shortcuts
[Introduce Apple Shortcuts as the first tool, connecting it to Automate from the opening. Use the supplied screenshot in the MacBook frame. The ribbon arrow points to the right-hand “What do you want your shortcut to do?” panel.]

▶ Click: the student notetaking example.

slides.title: Student notetaking
slides.notes:
B10b · Student notetaking
[Show the example you created in Shortcuts to support student notetaking. The left iPad shows the notes output, the centre iPad shows the Class Notes shortcut, and the right iPad shows the notes share sheet with Class Notes.]

▶ Click: your turn.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.notes:
B11 · Your turn
Your turn. Take your one-sentence problem from Round 2 and rewrite it with this template:
Blank can't blank. The blank has to happen at the same time as blank.
Then sketch it. Three minutes. Boxes and arrows.
Answer three questions:
What does the student see first?
What can they do on it?
What happens when they tap?
[Use the next scene’s three-minute timer.]

▶ Click: start the sketch timer.

slides.title: Sketch timer
slides.notes:
B11a · Sketch timer
[Give the room the full three minutes to sketch. The reminder reads: Sketch it. Boxes and arrows.]
[The supplied Shape of You instrumental accompanies the countdown. Wordless line imagery resolves into Ed Sheeran’s portrait from the supplied reference. The music fades during the last two seconds, then the completed frame holds until you advance.]

▶ Click: your prompt.

slides.title: Prompt spine
slides.notes:
B13 · Prompt spine
This is your prompt. Fill in the blanks from your sketch:
Build a single-screen tool for a Grade blank student who blank.
Show blank first, then let them blank.
Keep the language at blank. No sign-in.
Write it down. You'll paste it in a minute, and it stays on the build slide too.

▶ Click: examples.

slides.title: Examples
slides.notes:
B14 · Examples
Here are examples of what we can explore: interactives, explainer videos and Agentic updates.
And your materials are the boundary: it works from what you give it.
Today we will explore a small Web App. We are not promising a completed app.

[Before you go on, pair up. Say what it's for before anyone moves: everyone works with someone whose habits are different from theirs.
Have everyone line up by how much of their week already runs through an AI tool: "never" at one end, "it's in everything" at the other.
Then fold the line: the front person pairs with the back, second with second-last.]

▶ Click: chatbots and Gemini.

slides.title: Gemini
slides.notes:
B14a · Chatbots · Gemini
Introduce chatbots using Gemini as the presenter's chosen example.
[Supplied Gemini screenshot: Turtle Art coding-platform prompt and generated artifact.]

▶ Click: Biology example.

slides.title: Biology
slides.notes:
B14B · Biology
Here's what this can look like when you keep going.
This is a Grade 9 biology resource I built: the readings, a glossary that shows how the words connect, and a body index.
It's at dbbudd.github.io/biology if you want to explore it later.
You're not building this today. You're building the first, smallest version of yours.

▶ Click: BUILD 01.

slides.title: Build 01
slides.notes:
B15 · BUILD 01 · Web App · 15 minutes
Fifteen minutes to build a Web App.
One of you drives, one of you talks. Your prompt is bottom left.
Your first version will be wrong. That's the point. Go.
[The next board has the matching fifteen-minute timer and supplied FOLHK music mix.]

slides.title: Web App timer
slides.notes:

One drives. One talks.
[Fifteen-minute timer with the full supplied FOLHK mix at its original level and speed. Song-led line imagery follows Black Skinhead, The Pretender and Dani California, finishing on the supplied three-singer portrait. The last half-second hold is quiet.]

▶ Click: TEST 01.

slides.title: Test 01
slides.notes:
B16 · TEST 01 · Web App · 4 minutes
Stop building. Swap devices with another pair.
They use it cold. You say nothing.
Watch where they hesitate.
[Start a 4-minute timer.]

▶ Click: what it couldn't do.

slides.title: Couldn't do
slides.notes:
B17 · What it couldn't do
With your partner: what did you want it to do that it wouldn't?
[Give them a minute, then take answers and write them on the slide with the pen.]

▶ Click: SCAMPER.

slides.title: Scamper
slides.notes:
B17Sa · SCAMPER
Here's a tool for pushing an idea further: SCAMPER.
Substitute. Combine. Adapt. Modify. Put to another use. Eliminate. Reverse.

▶ Click: today's three.

slides.title: Scamper
slides.notes:
B17Sb · Today's three
Today we'll use three of them: Substitute, Combine and Eliminate.

▶ Click: the corners.

slides.title: Three corners
slides.notes:
B18 · Three corners
This is the room from above. The bar at the top is this screen.
Each corner is one move: Substitute, Combine, Eliminate.
And if yours already works, take the fourth corner: push it.
Change one thing.
[Give them four minutes to swap ideas with the others in their corner; the next board manages the time.]

slides.title: SCAMPER timer
slides.notes:

Substitute - Combine - Eliminate - Push It!
[Four-minute countdown. Rolling in the Deep imagery leads to Adele from the supplied reference. The activity instruction stays visible. The supplied Rolling in the Deep instrumental plays at its original speed, fades out, and is padded with silence to complete the four minutes.]

slides.title: Web app to agents
slides.notes:
B19b · Agents can

Access Local Files. Create Skills. Automate Workflows.

▶ Click: three words.

slides.title: Three words
slides.notes:
B12 · Three words
Three words before we explore Agents.
An app is anything you open and use. It doesn't need to be in an App Store.
HTML is the structure: boxes, text, where things sit.
JavaScript is the behaviour: what happens when you press the thing.
You write neither. You describe the behaviour.

slides.title: Build 02

Eight minutes, with agents. Swap roles: whoever talked now drives.
Same barrier. More ambition.
Nobody finishes this. You're finding out if it's buildable. Go.
